blocks.text: Output filtering checks a model response specifically for security concerns, signs a jailbreak or injection actually succeeded, leaked sensitive data, disallowed content, before it ever reaches the user, a distinct concern from the structural and semantic output validation covered in an earlier module.

This topic covers how output filtering differs from output validation, detecting signs of a successful attack in the response itself, redacting sensitive data, blocking disallowed content categories, and the real risk of overly aggressive filtering blocking legitimate responses.
1. Output Filtering as the Last Check Before the User

blocks.alt: Building on input validation, output filtering is the last check before delivery to the user

blocks.text: Output filtering is a security focused check applied to a model response right before it reaches the actual user, specifically looking for signs that something went wrong from a security standpoint, not just whether the response is well formed.
2. Output Filtering vs Output Validation

blocks.alt: Output validation checks structural and semantic correctness, output filtering here is a security focused check

blocks.text: Output validation, covered in an earlier module, checks whether a response is structurally correct and semantically reasonable, output filtering asks a different question, does this response show any sign of a security problem, a successful injection, leaked sensitive information, disallowed content, these checks are complementary, not overlapping.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Check","Primary Concern"],"rows":[["Output validation","Is the response structurally and semantically correct"],["Output filtering","Does the response show a security problem"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Detecting Signs of a Successful Injection

blocks.alt: A response showing signs of a successful injection gets caught before delivery

blocks.text: This connects directly to prompt injection and jailbreak attacks, both covered earlier in this module, a response that suddenly abandons its expected persona, format, or scope can be a signal the underlying prompt was actually manipulated, checking for these signs before delivery catches an attack that got past earlier defense layers.
4. Redacting Leaked Sensitive Data

blocks.alt: A sensitive data pattern gets detected and redacted from the response

blocks.text: This connects directly to data leakage, a topic already existing in this course covering this concern in depth, output filtering can include pattern based detection for common sensitive data shapes, redacting anything matching before the response actually reaches the user, an important last line of defense against accidental exposure.
5. Blocking Disallowed Content Categories

blocks.alt: A disallowed content category gets blocked outright

blocks.text: This connects directly to safety instructions, covered in an earlier module, output filtering provides a separate, independent check for disallowed content categories, functioning as a backstop in case a safety instruction alone did not fully prevent the model from generating something it should not have.

blocks.title: This backstop matters precisely because prompt level instructions are not perfect
blocks.content: The earlier Jailbreak Attacks topic covered why no single instruction fully prevents every attempt, output filtering provides an independent check that does not depend entirely on the prompt level instruction having worked correctly.

blocks.text: 6. Filtering as a Pipeline Step

blocks.alt: Output gets generated, a filter check gets applied, then it gets delivered to the user

blocks.text: Output filtering fits as an explicit step in a response pipeline, generate the response, apply the filter check, only then deliver it to the user, this connects directly to the tool execution validation pattern covered in the earlier Agent Prompting module, checking before committing to an action, applied here to the final response itself.
7. The Risk of Overly Aggressive Filtering

blocks.alt: Overly aggressive filtering blocks legitimate, safe responses

blocks.text: A filter tuned too aggressively, flagging too broadly, can end up blocking entirely legitimate, safe responses, a false positive rate that is too high genuinely degrades the actual user experience, this connects directly to the balanced safety concern covered in the earlier Safety Instructions topic, filtering needs the same careful calibration.
8. A Worked Output Filtering Example

A customer support system applies output filtering that checks every response against a pattern matching common sensitive data shapes, account numbers, before delivery, catching a rare case where a model response inadvertently included a specific account number it should not have surfaced, and redacting it automatically before the user ever sees it.
9. Output Filtering as the Last Line of Defense

This closes the security loop covered across this module so far, input validation and sanitization protect what comes in, safety instructions and guardrails, covered in the next topic, shape behavior during generation, and output filtering provides one final check on what actually goes out, catching what earlier layers may have missed.
Worked Example

A team building a document analysis assistant adds output filtering that checks every response for common sensitive data patterns before delivery, during testing this catches a case where an uploaded document, despite the input validation and sanitization layers already in place, still resulted in a response inadvertently repeating back a sensitive detail from the source document.

This output level catch, redacting the sensitive detail before the response reaches the user, demonstrates why a layered defense matters, the earlier layers reduced risk substantially but did not eliminate it entirely, and output filtering caught what got through.
Common Mistakes

items: Relying only on output validation for correctness while never checking output for genuine security concerns
Tuning a filter so aggressively that it blocks a meaningful number of legitimate, safe responses
Not treating output filtering as an independent backstop, assuming prompt level safety instructions alone are sufficient
Applying output filtering inconsistently rather than as a mandatory step every response passes through before delivery

blocks.text: Practice

Design an output filter for an application you have built or could build, specifying at least one check for a sensitive data pattern and one check for a disallowed content category, and consider what false positive rate would be acceptable before the filter starts meaningfully degrading legitimate user experience.
Key Takeaway

Output filtering checks a model response specifically for security concerns, signs of a successful attack, leaked sensitive data, disallowed content, right before delivery to the user, functioning as an independent backstop distinct from output validation and calibrated carefully to avoid blocking legitimate responses through excessive false positives.
